posts.title: The autumn batch leaves the fire
posts.excerpt: Twelve gyuto and eight nakiri, forged over three cold mornings. A week at the anvil with Isamu as the autumn batch takes shape.
posts.content:
The first cold week of October is the best week to forge. The workshop holds its heat, the steel moves slowly under the hammer, and Isamu can read its colour without the summer glare from the door.

Three mornings at the anvil

Every blank starts as a short bar of white carbon steel laid on soft iron. At the fire the two are welded into one, then drawn out, flattened and shaped. By the third morning there are twenty rough blades cooling on the rack, dark and scaled, nothing like knives yet.

You hear a good weld before you see it. The sound goes quiet.

Isamu Tanabe, at the anvil

Next week they go to Kenji at the wheel, then to Mio at the bench. The batch reaches the shop at the end of the month; readers of the letter see it two days early.

posts.title: How to sharpen on a 1000 stone, in ten minutes
posts.excerpt: Soak, set the angle, count your strokes. Mio's ten-minute routine for keeping a kitchen knife sharp at home.
posts.content:
Most home cooks need one stone: a 1000. Used three or four times a year, it keeps a good knife cutting like new. Here is the routine Mio teaches at the counter.

Ten minutes, start to finish

  • Soak the stone for ten minutes, until the bubbles stop.
  • Set it on a damp cloth so it cannot slide.
  • Hold the blade at about fifteen degrees: two coins under the spine.
  • Ten strokes on the first side, edge leading, light pressure.
  • Feel for the burr along the whole edge, then turn the knife over.
  • Finish with five lighter strokes per side, then wash and dry.

If the edge will not come back, it may need the coarse stone or a visit to the forge. Our care service sharpens any kitchen knife from $28.

posts.title: Why we cut on hinoki
posts.excerpt: A soft, fragrant cypress board is the kindest thing you can buy for a hard Japanese edge. Kenji on choosing, using and planing one.
posts.content:
A Japanese knife is hard, and a hard edge is brittle. Cut on glass, stone or bamboo and it chips. Cut on hinoki and the board gives a little under the edge, closes up again, and the edge lasts weeks longer.

Choosing a board

Look for a thick board with straight, even grain and no knots in the middle. Ours are 3 cm thick, planed by hand from offcuts of the sawmill next door.

Keeping it

Wet the board before you cut, so it takes fewer stains. Wash with water and a brush, stand it on its edge to dry, and once a year plane or sand it flat again.

posts.title: A morning at the grinding wheel
posts.excerpt: After the fire, the wheel. Kenji has ground every blade at the forge for twenty years. What he looks for, and why it takes so long.
posts.content:
The grinding room is the quietest part of the forge. Three stone wheels, two long benches, and a shaft of light from the high window that Kenji uses to read the bevel.

Grinding takes a knife from thick to thin: from a rough, dark blank to a blade that flexes very slightly at the tip. Too little and it wedges in a carrot; too much and the edge will not last.

The wheel tells you everything. You just have to stop talking.

Kenji Arata, at the wheel

posts.title: The care bench: what comes back to us
posts.excerpt: Chipped tips, rounded edges, a knife that met a dishwasher. A week of the sharpening service, and what each knife needed.
posts.content:
Every week a few dozen knives come back to the forge in small boxes. Some are ours, many are not. All of them leave sharp.

This week on the bench

  • A gyuto with a broken tip: reground to a new point, $45.
  • A twenty-year-old santoku, never sharpened: three stones and an hour.
  • A petty knife that went through a dishwasher: new edge, oiled handle.
  • Two nakiri from a restaurant down the street: they come back every month.

If your knife needs care, write to us with its length and what happened. Mio replies with a price and a booking number.

posts.title: Which knife first? Gyuto, santoku or petty
posts.excerpt: If you are buying one good knife, which should it be? A short guide to the three blades we sell most.
posts.content:
People ask this at the counter every day. The honest answer: the one that fits your hand and your cooking. But there are a few rules of thumb.

The gyuto

The all-rounder. Long enough for a cabbage and a joint of meat, fine enough for herbs. If you cook a lot, start here.

The santoku

Shorter and flatter, with a straight edge that likes chopping vegetables. Easy to control in a small kitchen.

The petty

A small knife for the hand: fruit, shallots, garlic, trimming. Everyone ends up with one, so it can wait.

products.name: Gyuto 210
products.short: The all-round chef knife: a white carbon steel core in soft iron, hand-ground thin, with an octagonal hinoki handle.
products.description:
Our best-loved knife and the one we suggest first. The carbon core is forge-welded between soft iron, hammered thin behind the edge and ground on the big wheel, so it slips through an onion and holds its edge for months.

Wash and dry it after use, cut on wood, and send it back to us when it needs an edge. The first resharpening is free.

products.name: Santoku 165
products.short: A flat, forgiving all-purpose knife with a blue carbon core: quick through vegetables, fish and meat.
products.description: Shorter and flatter than the gyuto, the santoku likes a straight up-and-down chop and is easy to control in a small kitchen. The blue carbon core is a little tougher than white steel and very forgiving to sharpen.

products.name: Petty 135
products.short: A small knife for the hand: fruit, shallots, garlic and trimming. Stainless-clad, so it forgives a wet board.
products.description: The knife everyone ends up reaching for. A carbon core clad in stainless steel, so only the very edge needs drying straight away. Light, nimble and a good first Japanese knife to give.

products.name: Nakiri 165
products.short: A tall, square vegetable knife with a dark kurouchi forge finish and a dead-flat edge for paper-thin slices.
products.description: The nakiri does one thing beautifully: vegetables. Its flat edge meets the board along its whole length, so daikon, cucumber and cabbage come away in clean, even slices. The dark forge scale is left on the upper blade, the way it came from the fire.

products.name: Whetstone Set 1000 / 6000
products.short: A medium 1000 stone and a fine 6000 polishing stone on a hinoki base, with a card of Mio's ten-minute routine.
products.description: Everything you need to keep a kitchen knife sharp at home. Soak the 1000 for ten minutes, sharpen, then finish on the 6000 for a polished, lasting edge. The hinoki base keeps the stones steady on the counter.

products.name: Hinoki Board
products.short: A thick board of soft, fragrant Japanese cypress that is kind to a fine edge. Planed by hand.
products.description:
Hinoki gives slightly under the knife and closes again, so a hard Japanese edge stays sharp far longer than on bamboo or plastic. Kenji planes every board by hand from offcuts of the sawmill next door.

Wet the board before use, wash with water, and stand it on its edge to dry.

products.name: Hand Sharpening Service
products.short: Send any kitchen knife back to the forge: sharpened by hand on stones and returned within ten days.
products.description:
Book a sharpening for one kitchen knife up to 210 mm. After checkout we send you a booking number and packing notes. Mio sharpens it on four stones, photographs the edge and returns it oiled and wrapped.
